Enhanced solubilization of solid organics and methane production by
anaerobic digestion of swine manure under nano-bubble water addition
Yujie Fana, Zhongfang Leia, Zitao Guoa, Weiwei Huangb, Di Wanga, Xuezhi Wanga,
Zhenya Zhanga, Kazuya Shimizua,⁎
a Graduate School of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan
b College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Forestry, Hainan University, Renmin Road, Haikou 570228, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Nano-bubble water
Anaerobic digestion
Swine manure
Methane production
Hydrolysis
A B S T R A C T
Nano-bubble water (NBW) refers to water with a large number of nanoscale particle bubbles. The aim of this
work was to study the mechanism of NBW addition into the anaerobic digestion (AD) of swine manure (SM). The
results showed that the cumulative methane production from the NBW added reactor was 192–225 mL/g-VS and
19–39% higher than the control group (without NBW addition). Based on the analysis of soluble organics, NBW
addition not only accelerated hydrolysis rates of proteins and carbohydrates, but also enhanced the production
of VFAs. Moreover, mechanism analysis reveals that NBW with higher spin–spin relaxation time and absolute
value of zeta potential might promote enzyme activity and the hydrolysis of organic solids. Simultaneously, the
electron transport system activity of the methanogenic communities and electric conductivity were enhanced by
NBW addition. This work implies that NBW addition is promising for enhancing AD for enhancement of methane
production.
1. Introduction
Globally, a large amount of livestock manure from animal hus-
bandry needs to be scientiﬁcally and eﬀectively processed. The annual
livestock waste produced in Japan is about 80 million tons, of which
swine manure (SM) is as high as 21 million tons (MAFF, 2018). If these
huge amounts of SM are not treated properly, not only the biomass
resources are wasted, but also the surrounding environments are pol-
luted. Composting is a widely applied method to handle livestock
manure since it is capable of stabilizing organic matters, increasing the
manure fertility and sterilizing weed seeds and pathogens (Yuan et al.,
2017). However, composting has some disadvantages like excessive
nutrients loss, greenhouse gases emission, and high eutrophication
potential (Yuan et al., 2018).
Anaerobic digestion (AD) has been widely used in the treatment of
SM. AD involves a series of biochemical processes, in which anaerobic
microorganisms can degrade and stabilize organic matters and produce
biogas and other valuable intermediates as well (Raposo et al., 2009).
Compared with other traditional treatment methods such as com-
posting, AD of SM has many advantages, such as water pollution re-
duction, generation of valuable bioenergy and fertilizer, odor control,
pathogen inactivation (Atandi and Rahman, 2012). Although the AD
process also produces CO2, the carbon source is not derived from fossil
fuel but from biomass, which is considered as carbon neutral (Kothari
et al., 2014). Therefore, AD has become a hot topic in the treatment of
SM. However, AD of SM also has some shortcomings, such as prone to
inhibition, low hydrolysis rate, low biogas and methane production
(Burton et al., 2003; Carrère et al., 2009).
Many methods can be used to increase methane production and to
improve AD performance, such as chemical (González-Fernández et al.,
2008), thermal (Wu et al., 2017), thermal steam explosion pretreatment
(Ferreira et al., 2014), co-digestion (Dennehy et al., 2016), initial pH
adjustment (Zhang et al., 2015), additives addition (Wang et al., 2017;
Yang et al., 2018), or applying a proper inoculum ratio (González-
Fernández and García-Encina, 2009). Although these methods show
some improvement eﬀects on AD performance, most of them have not
been applied in industry. The main reason is most probably due to the
consumption of chemicals and energy or the complexity of operations,
partly counteracting its environmental-friendliness and cost-eﬀective-
ness. As known, water is critical in the AD process, which can facilitate
the transfer of hydrolyzed products to the site where the bacteria can
utilize them (Bollon et al., 2013). In this aspect, most studies have been
focusing on water content, namely, AD performance under diﬀerent
total solids (TS) contents (dry or wet AD) (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al.,

2015). Few of them could be found on the eﬀects of water type and
characteristics on AD performance. Nano-bubble water (NBW) refers to
water with a large number of nanoscale particle bubbles. NBW is
characterized by its reduced friction and consequently increasing the
solubility of gases in liquids and producing free radicals (Liu et al.,
2013). Because of its unique characteristics, NBW has been successfully
applied in many ﬁelds, such as water puriﬁcation (Kyzas et al., 2019;
Agarwal et al., 2011), and medicine (Thakur et al., 2019). One recent
preliminary trial found that adding NBW to the digester treating waste
activated sludge could increase the methane production (Wang et al.,
2019). Although this preliminary research did not conduct a speciﬁc
study of the four stages of AD and did not analyze the changes in or-
ganic and inorganic substances in the AD process. This work is en-
couraging further research on the application eﬀect of NBW in AD.
However, little information is available on the eﬀect of NBW in AD, not
to mention the analysis of AD process and mechanisms involved under
NBW addition.
The purpose of the present study was to investigate the eﬀect of
NBW on AD of SM, aiming at exploring a new method to improve AD
performance rather than using conventional methods such as chemical
addition, thermal treatment and co-digestion. In order to study the
mechanisms of NBW in AD of SM, this study measured the spin–spin
relaxation times (T2) and zeta potential of NBW used in the AD process
and analyzed the related key enzymes. To better understand the ki-
netics of AD process and then analyze AD performance, kinetic mod-
eling was also applied in this study. To the best of our knowledge, this
was the ﬁrst systematic research on the eﬀects of NBW addition on
organics conversion, enzyme activity and the mechanisms involved in
the AD process. In addition, this work was also the ﬁrst study on the
application of NBW in the AD process of livestock manure.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Characterization of NBW
Three kinds of NBW were prepared, namely air-NBW (Air-NBW),
hydrogen-NBW (H2-NBW), and carbon dioxide-NBW (CO2-NBW). The
gases (Air, H2 and CO2) were introduced into deionized water (DW)
through a nano-bubble generator (HACK FB11, Japan) for 20 min at
20 ± 2 °C to obtain three kinds of NBW based on a previous study
(Wang et al., 2019). The zeta potential of NBW was detected by the Zeta
Potential Analyzer (MALVERN, Nano ZS, United Kingdom). The electric
conductivity was measured by an electric conductivity meter (AS-ONE

China). The spin–spin relaxation times (T2) were measured according to
a previous research (Liu et al., 2013), in which a pulsed NMR (JNM-
MU25A, JEOL, Japan) was used.
2.2. Batch AD experiments
2.2.1. Raw swine manure and inoculum
Raw SM was collected from a pig farm located in Tsukuba, Ibaraki,
Japan. The pigs were fed with corn, soybean, bran, and so on. After
manually sorting to remove large particles, such as small stones, plas-
tics and small clods, the raw SM was mixed thoroughly to ensure its
homogeneity and obtain the representative manure sample. The
manure sample was then stored at 4 °C in a refrigerator before AD
experiments. Main characteristics of the raw SM and seed AD sludge
(inoculum) are shown in Table 1.
2.2.2. Batch AD tests
All batch AD experiments were performed in a series of 250 mL
Scott Duran bottles, which were labeled as RControl, RNBW-Air, RNBW-H2
and RNBW-CO2 when the added water was DW, Air-NBW, H2-NBW, and
CO2-NBW, respectively (Table 2). Each 250 mL bottle was loaded with
20 g RSM and 80 g inoculum. In this research, 100 mL NBW or DW was
added at the beginning of the experiment. Two bottles only containing
inoculum were also tested in this work. As pH adjustment before AD
may have some impact on the microbial communities of raw SM, all the
initial sample pH before AD experiments were not adjusted in this
study. After being loaded with all the materials, the bottles were sealed
using rubber stoppers. All the reactors were ﬂushed with N2 for 3 min
and then put these reactors in an incubator (35 ± 2 °C) for 28 days
based on the preliminary experiments. The bottles were shaken
manually for 2 min once per day at a ﬁxed time before gas production
measurement. In this research, each AD test was conducted in duplicate
and eight bottles were sacriﬁced for sampling and analysis every four
days, four of which were parallel groups.

Total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), total nitrogen (TN) and total
ammonia nitrogen (TAN) were determined by the standard method
(APHA, 2012). P was determined according to Standards, Measure-

Analyzer, USA). Soluble carbohydrates concentration was measured by
using the Phenol-sulfuric method. Soluble proteins concentration was

Biogas (CH4 + CO2 + H2) production was determined using a gas

To explore the mechanisms involved in AD with the addition of
NBW, the activities of six enzymes, including coenzyme F420, dehy-
drogenase, protease, α-glucosidase, acid phosphatase (ACP) and alka-
line phosphatase (ALP), were examined individually in the experi-
ments. Coenzyme F420 and dehydrogenase were tested every 4 days
during the AD. The other four enzymes were measured on day 4.
Coenzyme F420 was measured by using the ultraviolet spectro-
photometry method (Hutschemackers et al., 1982). Dehydrogenase
activity was tested by using the TTC-Dehydrogenase method (Klapwijk
et al., 1974). Protease, α-glucosidase, ALP and ACP were measured
according to the literatures (Goel et al., 1998; Yuan et al., 2017).
Brieﬂy, protease was determined by using casein (10 mg/mL) as the
substrate and 0.4 M trichloroacetic acid (TCA) was used to terminate
the reaction. The p-nitrophenyl phosphate disodium salt (pnpP) of 0.1%
was used as the substrate for the determination of ALP and ACP. The p-
nitrophenyl-a-D-glucopyranoside (pnpG) of 0.1% was used as the sub-
strate for the determination of α-glycosidase.

2.4. Statistical analysis
For AD experiments and characterization tests for NBW, mean va-
lues from six repetitions of analysis were reported based on three par-
allel trials by using Microsoft Oﬃce Excel 2016. One-way analysis of
variance (ANOVA) was also applied for statistical analysis. Signiﬁcant
diﬀerence was set at p < 0.05. Multiple comparison analysis was used
paired t-test with Bonferoni to ﬁnd the most eﬀective NBW for methane
production. Signiﬁcant diﬀerence was set at p < 0.0083.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Biogas production and methanogenesis performance
Biogas and methane productions were evaluated in the batch tests
to study the eﬀect of NBW addition on AD of SM. As shown in Fig. 1, the
cumulative biogas and methane productions from RNBW were higher
than those from RControl. For the cumulative biogas production (Fig. 1a),
RNBW-H2, RNBW-CO2 and RNBW-Air achieved 378, 345 and 333 mL/g-VS,
respectively, corresponding to 31.5%, 20.1% and 16.1% increase when
compared with RControl. In terms of cumulative methane production
(Fig. 1b), RNBW-H2, RNBW-CO2 and RNBW-Air achieved 225, 195 and
192 mL/g-VS, respectively, increasing by 39.3%, 20.8% and 19.1% in
comparison to RControl. The cumulative methane production from RNBW-
H2 was signiﬁcantly higher than that from RControl.
The above results indicated that NBW addition promoted the pro-
duction of biogas and methane from the AD of SM. This might be due to
the addition of NBW promoted the hydrolysis of organic solids and
shortened the lag period, which was beneﬁcial to the subsequent
acidiﬁcation stage and methanogenesis stage. The enhancement in
methane yield might also be due to the addition of NBW enhanced the
activity of methanogens enzyme activity in the anaerobic digestion
reactor. Improvement in methane production was also likely to be the
result of the combination of these above factors. Therefore, the me-
chanisms involved in AD of SM under NBW addition requires further
analysis.

3.2. Soluble organics
Successful AD process must be able to eﬀectively degrade complex
substrate into methane, while various compounds may inhibit or pro-
mote AD process (Li et al., 2016). Proteins, carbohydrates and lipids in
organics contribute the most to methane production (Niu et al., 2014).
The content of lipids in SM is relatively low, < 1% COD (Lin et al.,
2015). Therefore, in this study, soluble proteins and carbohydrates
were selected as key research subjects. It could be found from Fig. 2a
that the soluble proteins in RNBW decreased rapidly in the later stages of
AD. However, the soluble proteins in RControl increased and reached a
maximum of about 720 mg/L. Fig. 2b shows the variation of soluble
carbohydrates. The trend of soluble carbohydrates was diﬀerent from
that of the soluble proteins. From the beginning to day 4, the soluble
carbohydrates in RNBW decreased rapidly, while that in RControl slowly
increased and reached its maximum (248 mg/L) on day 4. As the AD
progressed, the concentrations of soluble carbohydrates in RControl and
RNBW showed a downward trend.
At the beginning of the AD process, the VS contents in RControl and
RNBW were the same (Fig. 2c). Both RControl and RNBW showed a trend of
rapid decline and then slowly decline. However, the reduction rates of
VS in RNBW on day 4 (15.3–17.3%) and day 8 (30.5–35.2%) were faster
than those in RControl (9.8% on day 4, and 28.8% on day 8), which
indicated that the hydrolysis step in RNBW might be enhanced in com-
parison to that in RControl. The changes of soluble organics were the
results from the balance between hydrolysis and consumption. From the
results of soluble proteins and carbohydrates in this study, it could be
concluded that the soluble organics in RNBW were consumed faster than
those in RControl at the early stage of AD. Considering the changes of VS
at the initial stage of AD, it could be concluded that NBW addition not
only enhanced the hydrolysis rate, but also accelerated the consump-
tion rate of soluble organics. The consumption of soluble organics such
as soluble proteins and carbohydrates can produce VFAs (Wang et al.,
2014). Therefore, under NBW addition, the acidogenesis stage could be
promoted, too. After 16 days’AD, the VS reduction rate slowed down in
both RControl and RNBW. At the end of AD tests, there was no statistically
signiﬁcant diﬀerence in VS reduction rates between RControl and RNBW
(58.9–59.8% in RNBW and 57.2% in RControl, p > 0.05). By analyzing
the ﬁnal VS content, it was clear that NBW addition could not sig-
niﬁcantly enhance VS reduction. These results indicated that the yield

RNBW was more eﬃcient in using SM for methane production during

Fig. 2d illustrates the changes of sTOC in SM during 28 days’ AD
with or without NBW addition. Obviously, the sTOC ﬁrstly increased
and then decreased. At the beginning of the AD tests, the sTOC con-
centrations in RNBW were higher than that in RControl. As the AD pro-
gressed, the sTOC in RNBW decreased rapidly, which was basically
consistent with that in RControl during the late stage of AD. The max-
imum sTOC values in RNBW were 10.8–17.2% higher than that in
RControl. According to the above analysis, the consumption rates of so-
luble organics in RNBW were higher than RControl. Therefore, at the in-
itial stage of AD process, a higher sTOC concentration in RNBW than in
RControl also indicated that NBW addition enhanced the hydrolysis step.
VFAs include acetate (HAc), propionate (HPr), n-butyrate (n-HBu),
iso-butyrate (iso-HBu), n-valerate (n-HVa), and iso-valerate (iso-HVa),
which are products from hydrolysis and acidogenesis, and the sub-
strates for methanogenesis (Li et al., 2015). VFAs are mainly produced
in hydrolysis and acidogenesis stages of the AD process (Wang et al.,
2014). It could be found from Fig. 3 that the initial VFAs concentrations
in RControl and RNBW were almost at the same level, about 2100 mg/L.
When AD was progressed to day 4, the total concentrations of VFAs in
RNBW and RControl increased, and those in RNBW (2900–3100 mg/L) were
much higher than that in RControl (2700 mg/L). On day 8 and day 12,
VFAs might be rapidly consumed by methanogens and no VFAs in-
hibition phenomenon was observed. Therefore, the higher VFAs con-
centrations in RNBW at the early stage of AD might not be the result of
less consumption. Instead, it was attributable to a much faster hydro-
lysis, which was consistent with the results of methane production.
From day 4 to day 12, the methane production from RNBW was higher
than that of RControl by 25–53 mL/g-VS. Namely, NBW addition en-
hanced the hydrolysis and acidiﬁcation stages in the AD of SM. This
observation was also consistent with the results from the changes of VS
and soluble proteins/carbohydrates.
3.3. Eﬀects of NBW on related enzymes in AD process
The ﬂuorescent properties of coenzyme F420 have been used to
identify individual morphological types, colonies and growth rates of
methanogens (Reynolds and Colleran, 1987). It can be seen from the
Fig. 4a that the coenzyme F420 contents in RControl and RNBW increased
steadily during the ﬁrst 20 days, and then showed a downward trend.
The coenzyme F420 contents in RNBW were higher than RControl but the
diﬀerence was not so statistically signiﬁcant (p > 0.05). Moreover, the
diﬀerence among the three types of RNBW was also not obvious
(p > 0.05).
Dehydrogenase has the function of enzymatic dehydrogenation of
organic substances, which can reﬂect the number of active micro-
organisms and the degradation activity of organic substances. As seen
in Fig. 4b, the dehydrogenase activity in RNBW was higher than that in
RControl during the ﬁrst 12 days of the AD process. This observation
indicated that the activities of methanogen and dehydrogenase were
enhanced by NBW addition. In addition, four enzymes (protease, α-
glucosidase, ALP and ACP) were also measured to study the hydrolysis
process. On day 4, the activities of ALP, ACP, α-glucosidase and pro-
tease in RNBW were higher than those in RControl, which also indicated
that the hydrolysis process was enhanced due to the addition of NBW.
3.4. Changes in ETS and electric conductivity
ETS is associated with microbial respiratory activities in AD systems
(Yin et al., 2005). Therefore, ETS can reﬂect the biological activities of
microorganisms in the AD of SM. Fig. 5a shows the relative ETS in

3.6. Mechanisms involved in AD of SM under NBW addition
In this work, multiple parallel experiments demonstrated that NBW
addition could increase CH4 yield in the AD of SW. In terms of soluble
organics, the addition of NBW accelerated the VS reduction at the initial
stage of AD, indicating that the hydrolysis of SM was enhanced due to
NBW addition. Moreover, by analyzing the changes of VFAs and soluble
proteins/carbohydrates, it can be seen that NBW addition might en-
hance the hydrolysis and acidiﬁcation stages in the AD process.
However, the addition of NBW did not signiﬁcantly increase the VS
reduction rates when the entire AD process was considered. In addition,
NBW addition did not change the compositions of the inoculum and
raw SM, nor did it change carbon to nitrogen ratio.
In order to clarify the mechanisms of NBW addition for improving
AD of SM, the T2 and zeta potential were analyzed in this work. As
shown in Fig. 6, the T2 values in the three types of NBW (2803.49,
2873.21 and 3012.71 ms) were longer than that in DW (2459.21 ms),
and the maximum value of T2 was detected in H2-NBW. The relatively
long T2 value could be contributed by the weakening of the hydrogen-
bonding network in water, which increases the mobility of the water
molecules (Liu et al., 2013). That is, the hydrogen-bonding network in
RNBW was weaker and the mobility of the water molecules in RNBW was
stronger than that in RControl. As known, zeta potential plays a key role
in bubble stability (Parmar and Majumder, 2013). Colloids with high
zeta potential contribute to electrical stability and avoid coalescence
due to repulsion. As it can be expected, due to the addition of NBW, the
absolute value of zeta potential could be increased. In this study, since
NBW has a higher absolute value of zeta potential (16.5–21.1 mV) than
DW (1.7 mV), addition of NBW may avoid the formation of aggregates
and maintain the long-term electrical stability (Fig. 6). When NBs reach
the critical size, these bubbles will violently collapse during their
growth. As stated, cavitation collapse can not only produce li-
quid–vapor interface high pressure, strong local heating, high shear and
turbulence, but also free radicals (Bougrier et al., 2006).
The number of bubble particles was reported to be still around
1 × 108 particles/mL when NBW was stored for 14 days (Wang et al.,
2019). Therefore, when NBW was added to the AD of SM, NBW might
play its role in the AD process for a relatively long time. When NBW
with higher T2 value and zeta potential was added into the AD of SM,
the enzyme activities were improved. From the activities of the four
hydrolases (ALP, ACP, α-glucosidase and protease), it could be con-
cluded that addition of NBW increased the hydrolysis rates. This result
was consistent with the results from the kinetic model analysis.
Therefore, NBW addition promoted hydrolysis stage during AD of SM.
The increase in hydrolysis rate facilitates subsequent acidiﬁcation stage
and methanogenesis stage, which is beneﬁcial to increase methane
production and improve AD performance.
In addition, the changes of Coenzyme F420 contents indicated that
NBW addition increased the activity of methanogens. On the other
hand, the activity of dehydrogenase was also enhanced under NBW
addition. The enhanced enzyme activities might be accompanied by the
increased activities of microbial populations such as methanogens. The
changes in ETS and electric conductivity in RNBW could further conﬁrm
the improved activities of microbial population after NBW supple-
mentation, resulting in faster utilization of soluble organics and then
increased methane production.
Therefore, NBW with higher T2 value and the absolute value of zeta
potential made the solution in the AD reactor have higher mobility of
water molecules, weaker hydrogen-bonding network and higher elec-
tric conductivity, which could enhance the activities of methanogens
and related enzymes, thereby further increasing methane production
and improving AD performance. Results from this study suggested that
NBW supplementation might be a promising approach for AD of SM.
Future works are still demanding on the in-depth mechanisms of NBW
in the AD process, characteristics of the digestate, and the impact of its
application in farmland.
4. Conclusions
(1) Biogas and methane production were enhanced respectively by
16.1%-31.5% and 19.1%-39.3% under the addition of NBW.
(2) NBW addition was found to enhance the hydrolysis and acidiﬁca-
tion stages in the AD of SM.
(3) Coenzyme F420 and dehydrogenase were increased under NBW
addition, indicating the activities of methanogen and dehy-
drogenase were enhanced. ETS and electric conductivity were also
increased, signaling the enhanced activity of microorganisms.
(4) The increases in T2 and the absolute value of zeta potential reﬂected
the weaker hydrogen-bonding network and the greater mobility of
water molecules.
